activities.anchor: its modern machinery is more concrete than the word suggests
activities.caption: call the trade share before the reveal
activities.name: egTradeEstimate

config.prompt: World trade in goods and services stands at roughly what share of global output today?
config.why: Around 60 per cent — up from about a quarter in 1970, on container ships carrying over 20,000 standard units and rules agreed at the World Trade Organization; close to a billion people left extreme poverty between 1990 and the late 2010s, most of them in Asia, on globalised trade.

activities.anchor: show the middle of the sequence
activities.caption: file each economy under its sector signature
activities.name: egSectorSort

config.prompt: What people do for a living — file each fact:

items.label: roughly four million garment workers, the majority women, earning about 80% of Bangladesh's export earnings
the United Kingdom today: over 80% of jobs
India: over half of output earned here, manufacturing near 15%
unregistered work from street vending to gig platforms
undercounted by half or more in much of the developing world

config.why: The UK walked the path first and furthest — cotton and steel workshop in 1850 to a service economy — while India's jump from fields to services is Rodrik's 'premature deindustrialisation': software and business services can be exported without a factory stage.

activities.anchor: turned loading into craned steel boxes
activities.caption: call the cost collapse per ton
activities.name: egBoxEstimate

config.prompt: In 1956, handling a ship's cargo cost $5.86 per ton. After Malcolm McLean's standardized container, it cost about —?
config.why: About 16 cents — a cut of more than 90% (Levinson's accounting), scale enough that the Ever Given's 2021 grounding in the Suez Canal could hold up trade of the order of $10 billion a day.

activities.anchor: reach into agriculture as much as electronics
activities.caption: pair the governance cases with their lessons
activities.name: egCasesMatch

config.prompt: Two cases frame where production lands — pair each fact:

pairs.right: grown around Kenya's Lake Naivasha and flown out fresh
the same cheap air freight and cold chains that moved the phone
1,134 workers killed producing for Western brands

pairs.left: the template for binding supply-chain regulation
pairs.right: the Bangladesh Accord on factory safety

config.why: A TNC's map is a network of contracts, and the geography of responsibility does not automatically follow the geography of production — the brand's code of conduct versus the subcontracted building it never inspected.

config.prompt: Destinations age in a known order — line up the Butler life-cycle stages:
config.why: Benidorm is the standard worked case — fishing village to package-tourism archetype to high-rise rejuvenation. And the curve itself: about 25 million international arrivals in 1950, roughly 1.5 billion in 2019, a 70% collapse in 2020, recovery to about 1.4 billion in 2024.

activities.caption: true or false — tourists, money, locals
activities.name: egLeakageJudge

statements.s: Gross tourist spending is a good proxy for local income.
statements.why: Measure receipts net of leakage, seasonality and the low-wage structure of much tourism employment, and the link is far weaker than the arrivals chart suggests.

statements.s: Who owns the hotel changes what the destination keeps.
statements.why: Profits repatriated by foreign-owned chains drain away — the right questions are always: who owns it, where is the food bought, what share of the booking fee stayed.

statements.s: Food imported to feed hotels keeps local income high.
statements.why: It does the opposite — it is one of the three classic drains, with repatriated profits and booking-platform commissions.

statements.s: Overtourism's costs are real enough that Venice charges day-trippers an entry fee from 2024.
statements.why: €5 — a management response to a classic congestion problem, alongside Barcelona's protests; tourism's footprint is about 8% of global greenhouse-gas emissions, mostly from flights.

activities.caption: drag the divider — two openness ratios
activities.name: egOpennessCompare

config.prompt: Exports plus imports as a share of GDP — drag the divider:

before.label: Netherlands — above 150%
before.text: A small economy near the sea with big ports lives by re-exporting — goods cross the border twice on their way to you.

after.label: United States — around 25%
after.text: A continental economy produces for its own vast market.

config.why: The gap is not that the Dutch trade six times more enthusiastically — ratios measure exposure, not vitality. A serious answer to 'how globalised is this economy?' always asks: measured how, gross or value-added, relative to what.

activities.caption: run the central bank — sequence the opening
activities.name: egCapitalBranch

config.root: You run a developing economy's central bank. Capital now moves in seconds.

start.text: Foreign lenders are queueing. Open the capital account now?

choices.label: Open it now, banks can catch up later
choices.feedback: The sequencing error: economies that open capital accounts before their banking systems can bear it have repeatedly paid for it — reversals take months, not decades.

choices.label: Sequence it — strengthen the banks first
choices.feedback: Trade integration is stable and slow; the financial layer is volatile and fast — order matters more than speed.

end.text: Contagion travels by balance sheet, not by road — Asia 1997, 2008 and 2022 all share that geography, and it is why the IMF exists as a crisis lender.

config.why: Hot money reversed out of the 'tiger' economies within months in 1997; US mortgage defaults became a global banking freeze in 2008; the 2022 rate rises repriced every emerging-market debt overnight.
